profile.biography: Lianzijun (Lian) Wang is a Biology PhD student at Duke University in Dave Sherwood’s lab. Her research uses the C. elegans anchor cell invasion model to study how invasive cells breach basement membrane, reorganize their cytoskeleton, protect the plasma membrane, and adapt mitochondrial metabolism under mechanical challenge.

homeAbout.headline: Lianzijun Wang
homeAbout.subtitle: Research · Music · Exploration
story: I was born and raised in Kunming, Yunnan, China, a city nicknamed the City of Eternal Spring for its lovely year-round weather. Growing up surrounded by mountains, flowers, and some incredible food, I have always had a soft spot for nature and exploring the world around me.

There is also a little story behind my name. 莲 means lotus, 子 can mean seed, and together 莲子 means lotus seed. 君 is associated with noble character, while 子君 has a classical, scholarly ring to it. My name draws inspiration from 爱莲说 (On the Love of the Lotus), a Chinese essay that celebrates the lotus for growing out of muddy waters while remaining beautiful and untainted.

My own journey has taken me quite a distance from Kunming. I moved to the United States for college and earned my bachelor’s degree at Baylor University, where I studied Biochemistry and Cell & Molecular Biology. That is where I first fell in love with research in Dr. Myeongwoo Lee’s lab, working with C. elegans.
Now, I am a Biology PhD student at Duke University in Dr. Dave Sherwood’s lab. My research focuses on how cells break through the physical barriers around them.

Outside the lab, I love playing the pipa (琵琶), scuba diving, traveling, photography, snowboarding, and finding new ways to explore the world through a microscope, underwater, or somewhere I have never been before.
Welcome to my corner of the pond 🪷

items.heading: Ph.D. Researcher, Duke University
items.detail: Investigates how invasive cells breach basement membrane using the C. elegans anchor cell invasion model, with emphasis on perlecan, membrane protection, mitochondrial adaptation, spectrin, and mechanical resilience.
